title: From a Lot to a Diamond
bigQuestion: How did many loose bat-and-ball games become one baseball with a measured field?

story.title: Jackets on the Grass
story.kicker: Kids use jackets for bases, then walk past a field with white lines and a measured square.
paragraphs: It is a warm evening at a city park. Five kids want to play ball. They have one bat and one scuffed ball. They have no bases, so they drop their jackets on the grass. A red jacket is first base. A backpack is home.

The jackets land wherever someone tosses them. First base is close. Second base is far away by the fence. Nobody measured anything. The kids argue about whether a runner was safe. Each kid remembers the bases a little differently.

On the walk home, they pass the high school field. White chalk lines run out from home plate. Four white bases sit at the corners of a square. A sign on the dugout lists the school team's schedule against other towns.

The kids at the park made a game for one evening. The school field holds a game that strangers can share. Every base on that field sits ninety feet from the next one. Clubs in New York first agreed on that distance in the 1850s.
story.think: What changes when the bases are measured instead of tossed on the grass?

lessons.title: Rounders and Town Ball
lessons.mainIdea: People in England and America played many bat-and-ball games long before baseball had written rules.
reading: In England in the 1700s, children played bat-and-ball games with many names. One was *rounders*. A player hit a ball and ran around a loop of posts or stones. Another old game was stoolball, played with a stool as the target.

In 1744, a London printer named John Newbery sold a children's book called A Little Pretty Pocket-Book. It has a short rhyme and a small picture titled Base-Ball. This is one of the oldest printed uses of the word.

English settlers brought these games to North America. By the early 1800s, people in American cities played a game called *town ball*. The number of players, the bases and the ways to make an out changed from town to town.

words.d: an old English bat-and-ball game in which a hitter runs around a loop of posts
a bat-and-ball game played in American towns in the early 1800s, with rules that varied by place

look.title: A Rhyme from 1744

check.why: Town ball had no single rule book, so players, bases and outs varied by place.

lessons.title: A Ban Near a Meeting House
lessons.mainIdea: A 1791 town law from Pittsfield, Massachusetts, shows people were already playing baseball there.
reading: In 1791, the town of Pittsfield, Massachusetts, passed a *bylaw*. A bylaw is a rule made by a town. It banned games of baseball and some other ball games within 80 yards of the new meeting house.

The town wanted to protect the windows of its meeting house. Broken glass was expensive. A town does not ban a game that nobody plays. So the bylaw tells historians that baseball was common enough to cause trouble.

Historians found this record in 2004 in old town papers. It is one of the oldest written uses of the word baseball in the United States. It shows the game grew slowly from many places, not from one inventor.

words.d: a rule made by a town or a club for its own members or land
a written paper kept from the past that historians can study

look.title: Reading a Ban

look.prompt: What can this ban tell you about what people did in Pittsfield in 1791?

check.q: What is a bylaw?
choices: a rule made by a town or a club
check.why: A bylaw is a rule a town or club makes for itself.

check.q: Why does the Pittsfield ban matter to historians?
choices: It names the inventor of baseball.
It shows baseball was already played in 1791.
It set the bases at 90 feet.
check.why: A town bans only a game people play, so the bylaw proves baseball was played there.

lessons.title: The Cooperstown Legend
lessons.mainIdea: The story that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in 1839 is a legend; no evidence supports it.
reading: In 1905, a group called the Mills Commission began studying where baseball came from. Albert Spalding, a sporting goods maker, pushed for it. He wanted to show that baseball was an American game, not an English one.

In 1907, the commission reported that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. Its main proof was a letter from one old man, Abner Graves. Doubleday himself never wrote that he made up the game.
Historians call this story a *legend*. In 1839 Doubleday was a cadet at West Point, far from Cooperstown. Still, the legend is why the National Baseball Hall of Fame opened in Cooperstown in 1939.

words.d: a story told as history that cannot be proven and may not be true
a group chosen to study a question and report on it
records or objects that show something really happened

look.title: One Letter, One Claim
look.text: Claim: Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839. Proof offered in 1907: one letter written many years later by a man who said he remembered it. Other records: a 1744 book page titled Base-Ball and a 1791 town ban on baseball.
look.prompt: Which records are stronger evidence about baseball's age, and why?

check.q: Which group named Doubleday as baseball's inventor in 1907?
check.why: The Mills Commission made that claim in its 1907 report.

check.q: Why do historians doubt the Doubleday story?
choices: Its main proof was one late letter, and Doubleday was at West Point in 1839.
check.why: The story rests on one letter, and Doubleday was a West Point cadet in 1839.

check.q: What opened in Cooperstown in 1939 because of the legend?
choices: the National Baseball Hall of Fame
check.why: The Hall of Fame opened in Cooperstown in 1939, tied to the legend's date.

lessons.title: The Knickerbocker Club
lessons.mainIdea: In 1845 the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York wrote down a short set of rules.
reading: In 1845, a group of young men in New York City formed the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club. Many were clerks and shopkeepers. They met to play in the afternoons. That year they wrote a list of twenty rules.
Alexander Cartwright was a member, and his name is often tied to those rules. Historians still argue about how much he wrote. Several members worked on the club's game together.
The Knickerbockers played at the *Elysian Fields* in Hoboken, New Jersey. It was a park across the river from New York. Open city land was scarce, so clubs rode a ferry to reach a big, flat field.

words.d: a group of members who meet, pay dues and follow their own rules
a park in Hoboken, New Jersey, where the Knickerbockers and other early clubs played

look.title: A Ferry to the Field
look.text: New York City in the 1840s. Streets are crowded with buildings and carts. A club packs bats and a ball, walks to the dock and pays for a ferry across the Hudson River. On the far side is a wide green park in Hoboken.
look.prompt: Why would a city club travel so far to find a place to play?

check.why: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club wrote its rules in 1845.

check.q: Where did the Knickerbockers play?
choices: the Elysian Fields in Hoboken, New Jersey
check.why: The club took a ferry to the Elysian Fields in Hoboken.

check.q: What do historians still argue about?
choices: whether the rules were written in English

check.why: Cartwright is linked to the rules, but his exact part is debated.

lessons.title: Paces on the Ground
lessons.mainIdea: The 1845 rules measured the bases in paces, which are steps, not in feet.
reading: The Knickerbocker rules said the bases would be 42 *paces* from home to second base. They also said 42 paces from first base to third base. A pace is a long walking step.
A pace is not an exact size. A tall person's step is longer than a short person's step. So historians are not sure how far apart the 1845 bases really were. Their guesses differ by many feet.

The rules also set a *foul* line idea. A ball hit outside the lines from home through first and third was foul. The rules also said a fielder could not throw the ball at a runner to get an out, which older games had allowed.

words.d: a long walking step, once used to measure distance
a hit ball that lands outside the lines of the field

look.title: Rule Four, 1845
look.text: The bases shall be from home to second base, forty-two paces; from first to third base, forty-two paces, equidistant.
look.cite: Rules of the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club, New York, 1845, rule 4
look.prompt: Why might two clubs draw different fields from this rule?

check.q: What is a pace?
check.why: A pace is a step, so its length changes with the person.

check.q: Why is a pace a weak way to measure a field?
choices: It is too long for any field.
Different people take steps of different lengths.
It was banned in New York.
check.why: Step length varies, so a field paced out by two people differs.

check.q: Which older practice did the 1845 rules stop?
choices: throwing the ball at a runner to get an out
check.why: The Knickerbocker rules did not allow fielders to hit runners with a thrown ball.

lessons.title: Ninety Feet
lessons.mainIdea: In 1857 New York clubs agreed on thirty yards, or ninety feet, between bases.
reading: By the 1850s, many clubs in and near New York played the Knickerbocker game. In 1857, clubs from the New York area met in a *convention* to agree on one set of rules. A convention is a meeting of groups who vote together.
The 1857 rules set the bases thirty yards apart. Thirty yards is ninety feet. The same meeting said a game would last nine innings. Before that, the first team to score 21 runs won.

In 1858, the clubs formed the National Association of Base Ball Players. It was the first group to govern many baseball clubs. Ninety feet between bases is still the rule for high school, college and major league baseball.

words.d: a meeting where clubs or groups vote on shared rules
a unit of length equal to three feet
a part of a baseball game in which each team gets a turn to bat

look.title: Base Paths Today
look.cite: Little League Baseball rules; NFHS Baseball Rules; Official Baseball Rules
look.prompt: At which levels do players use the ninety-foot distance from 1857?

check.q: How far apart are the bases under the 1857 rules?
check.why: The 1857 rules set thirty yards, which is ninety feet.

check.q: How did a game end before the 1857 rules set nine innings?
choices: The first team to score 21 runs won.
The game stopped at sunset only.
check.why: Early Knickerbocker games ended when a team reached 21 runs.

check.q: What group did clubs form in 1858?
choices: the National Association of Base Ball Players
check.why: The National Association of Base Ball Players formed in 1858.

lessons.title: Paid Players in Cincinnati
lessons.mainIdea: In 1869 the Cincinnati Red Stockings became the first openly all-professional baseball team.
reading: At first, baseball clubs were *amateur*. Players did not get paid to play. By the 1860s, some clubs quietly paid good players with jobs or cash. The rules of the national association did not allow it.
In 1869, the Cincinnati Red Stockings paid every player openly. Harry Wright ran the team. His brother George Wright played shortstop. They were the first openly all-*professional* baseball team.
The Red Stockings rode trains to play clubs in many cities, from the East Coast to California. They did not lose a game that season. Crowds everywhere saw the same field shape and rules.

words.d: a player who plays without being paid
a player who is paid to play as a job

look.title: A Train of Red Socks
look.text: Summer 1869. A team in bright red stockings steps off a train in a new city. Posters announce the game. The local club has lined its field the same way the visitors do at home in Cincinnati.
look.prompt: How would a traveling team help spread one set of field rules?

check.q: What made the 1869 Red Stockings different?
choices: They played only in New York.
They were a high school team.
check.why: The Red Stockings were the first openly all-professional team.

check.q: Who ran the 1869 Red Stockings?
check.why: Harry Wright ran the team; his brother George played for it.

check.q: What is an amateur?

check.why: An amateur plays for no pay.

lessons.title: A League in 1876
lessons.mainIdea: The National League, founded in 1876, set one schedule and one rule book for its clubs.
reading: In 1876, club owners formed the National League of Professional Base Ball Clubs. William Hulbert, who ran the Chicago club, led the plan. Eight cities had teams in the first season.

A *league* is a group of teams that agree to one schedule and one set of rules. The owners, not the players, controlled this league. They banned betting and drinking at games to make the sport look respectable.

The Chicago White Stockings won the first National League *pennant* in 1876. A pennant is the flag and title for a league champion. That Chicago club later became the team known today as the Chicago Cubs.

words.d: a group of teams that play one schedule under one set of rules
a flag and title given to a league's champion team

check.q: When was the National League founded?
check.why: Owners formed the National League in 1876.

check.q: Which team won the first National League pennant?
check.why: Chicago's White Stockings won the 1876 pennant.

check.q: Who controlled the new National League?
check.why: Owners, led by William Hulbert, ran the league.

lessons.title: The Pitcher Moves Back
lessons.mainIdea: Leagues moved the pitching distance from 45 feet to 50 feet in 1881 and to 60 feet 6 inches in 1893.
reading: Early rules put the pitcher 45 feet from home plate. Pitchers threw harder over the years. Batters had less and less time to see the ball, and scores dropped.
In 1881, the National League moved the pitcher back to 50 feet. From 1881 to 1892, pitchers threw from inside a marked *pitcher's box*. Leagues kept changing the rules to balance the game.

In 1893, the league set the distance at 60 feet 6 inches. The box was replaced by a rubber slab called the *pitcher's plate*. Batting improved right away. That distance is still the major league rule today.

words.d: a marked area pitchers threw from before 1893
the rubber slab that marks the pitching distance, used since 1893

check.q: What was the pitching distance from 1881 to 1892?
check.why: The National League used 50 feet from 1881 through 1892.

check.q: When did 60 feet 6 inches become the rule?
check.why: The 60 feet 6 inch distance dates from 1893.

check.q: Why did leagues move the pitcher back?
choices: Batters had too little time as pitchers threw harder.
check.why: Harder pitching made scores drop, so leagues gave batters more time.

lessons.title: Home Plate Gets Its Shape
lessons.mainIdea: In 1900 home plate became a five-sided slab 17 inches wide.
reading: Early home bases were often round or square. Some were iron or stone. By the 1870s, rules called for a square slab of white marble or stone. Its corner pointed toward the pitcher.

In 1900, the National League made home plate a five-sided shape called a *pentagon*. It is 17 inches wide across the front edge. The wide edge faces the pitcher, which made it easier for umpires to see the plate.
Today the same plate is set in fields at every level, from a park league to a major league stadium. The Official Baseball Rules include a drawing of the plate with every measurement.

words.d: the five-sided slab where a batter stands and runners score
a flat shape with five sides

look.title: Two Plates Side by Side
look.text: On the left: a square white slab from the 1870s, set with one corner toward the pitcher. On the right: a white five-sided plate from 1900, with a flat 17-inch edge toward the pitcher and a point toward the backstop.
look.prompt: Which plate gives an umpire a clearer front edge to look at, and why?

check.why: The National League adopted the five-sided plate in 1900.

check.q: How wide is the front edge of home plate?

lessons.title: Games in Army Camps
lessons.mainIdea: Soldiers played baseball in camps during the Civil War and carried the game home.
reading: The Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865. Soldiers spent long weeks waiting in camps. Men from New York and other cities brought the New York rules with them. They marked out fields near their tents.
Soldiers from farms and small towns learned the game in camp. Some prisoners of war also played. When the war ended, many men went home and started clubs in their own towns.
After the war, the number of clubs in the national association grew fast. Clubs in new states wrote to ask for the rules. A printed rule book let a club far from New York line its field the same way.

words.d: the war in the United States from 1861 to 1865 between the Union and the Confederacy
a printed list of a game's rules that groups agree to follow

look.title: A Field Beside the Tents
look.text: An army camp in 1862. Rows of white tents stand in a meadow. Two soldiers pace off bases on flat ground. One holds a small printed booklet of rules. Men from farms, who have never seen the game, stand and watch.
look.prompt: How could a war camp help a city game reach small towns?

check.q: When was the Civil War?
check.why: The Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865.

choices: Soldiers learned it in camps and took it home.

check.why: Men learned the game in camps and started clubs after the war.

lessons.title: One Field, Many Levels
lessons.mainIdea: Rule groups for children, schools and major leagues each publish field measurements.
reading: Today, different groups write baseball rules for different players. Major League Baseball publishes the Official Baseball Rules. The *NFHS*, the National Federation of State High School Associations, writes rules for high school games.

Little League Baseball began in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1939. Its fields for young players have bases 60 feet apart. The field is smaller, but it keeps the same diamond shape and the same order of bases.
Because each group prints its measurements, a visiting team knows what field it will find. A school team from Peoria and a team from Chicago can meet on a field lined to the same NFHS numbers.

words.d: National Federation of State High School Associations, which writes rules for many high school sports
a youth baseball organization founded in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, in 1939

look.title: What a Field Rule Says
look.text: The rule books describe the infield as a square 90 feet on each side, with home plate, first base, second base and third base at its corners.
look.cite: Official Baseball Rules, Rule 2.01 (the playing field)
look.prompt: Why does a rule book give exact numbers instead of saying the bases should be far apart?

check.q: What does NFHS stand for?
choices: National Federation of State High School Associations

check.why: NFHS is the National Federation of State High School Associations.
